stem: You want Dependabot to group related minor and patch updates into a single pull request to reduce noise. Which configuration supports this?

options.text: A groups setting in dependabot.yml
Setting open-pull-requests-limit to zero
Enabling push protection
Adding a CODEOWNERS entry

explanationCorrect: Dependabot supports a groups key in the configuration so that multiple related updates are combined into one pull request instead of many separate ones.
explanationIncorrect: Setting open-pull-requests-limit to zero would stop Dependabot from opening update pull requests at all, not group them. Push protection is a secret scanning feature unrelated to how update pull requests are batched. A CODEOWNERS entry routes reviews and does not change how Dependabot groups updates.

stem: Dependabot alerts distinguish direct from transitive dependencies. Why does that distinction matter for remediation?

options.text: A transitive vulnerability may require updating the direct dependency that pulls it in, not the transitive package directly
Transitive dependencies cannot be vulnerable
Direct dependencies are never scanned
Transitive dependencies must be vendored to be fixed

explanationCorrect: Because a transitive dependency is pulled in by another package, fixing it often means bumping the direct dependency to a version that resolves a patched transitive one, so knowing which is which guides the fix.
explanationIncorrect: Transitive dependencies certainly can be vulnerable; that is precisely why they are tracked. Direct dependencies are scanned as well, so claiming they are never scanned is false. Vendoring is not a requirement to fix a transitive dependency; updating the chain that brings it in is the usual path.

stem: Which of these does Dependabot need to determine your dependencies for an ecosystem like npm?

options.text: The manifest and lockfile such as package.json and package-lock.json
A running instance of the application
A CODEOWNERS file
The compiled production bundle only

explanationCorrect: Dependabot reads the ecosystem's manifest and lockfile, for example package.json and package-lock.json, to know which packages and versions your project depends on.
explanationIncorrect: It performs static analysis of dependency files and does not need a running instance of the application. A CODEOWNERS file is about review routing and tells Dependabot nothing about dependencies. The compiled production bundle alone typically obscures the declared dependency versions Dependabot relies on, so the manifest and lockfile are what it uses.

stem: Which three capabilities are the core pillars of GitHub Advanced Security?

options.text: Code scanning, secret scanning, and dependency review/Dependabot
Pages, Projects, and Discussions
Actions, Packages, and Codespaces
Wiki, Insights, and Releases

explanationCorrect: GHAS centers on code scanning for vulnerable code, secret scanning for leaked credentials, and supply-chain security via the dependency graph, Dependabot, and dependency review.
explanationIncorrect: Pages, Projects, and Discussions are collaboration and publishing features, not security scanning. Actions, Packages, and Codespaces are automation, artifact hosting, and development environments, not the GHAS security pillars. Wiki, Insights, and Releases are documentation, analytics, and distribution features unrelated to the security capabilities GHAS provides.

stem: For public repositories on GitHub.com, which statement about GHAS features is accurate?

options.text: Code scanning, secret scanning, and dependency features are available at no cost
GHAS features are never available on public repositories
Only paid organizations can use them on public repos
They require a self-hosted server

explanationCorrect: On public repositories these security features are offered free of charge, which is why open-source projects can use code scanning, secret scanning, and dependency review without a GHAS license.
explanationIncorrect: They are available on public repositories, so the claim that they never are is wrong. They do not require a paid organization for public repos; the free availability is exactly the point. They do not require a self-hosted server; these run on GitHub.com for public repositories.

stem: In an enterprise, how is a GHAS license typically consumed?

options.text: Per active committer to repositories where GHAS features are enabled
Per repository regardless of contributors
Per workflow run
Per gigabyte of code scanned

explanationCorrect: GHAS is licensed by unique active committers on repositories with the features enabled, so the same person committing to several enabled repositories still consumes one seat.
explanationIncorrect: It is not billed simply per repository; the seat model counts committers, so one repo with many committers or many repos with one committer bill differently. It is not billed per workflow run; that is closer to Actions minute billing, a separate meter. It is not billed per gigabyte of scanned code; volume of code is not the licensing unit.

stem: Where can an organization see an aggregated view of code scanning, secret scanning, and Dependabot alerts across repositories?

options.text: The Security overview
The Insights tab
The Actions tab
The Packages page

explanationCorrect: The Security overview aggregates alerts from code scanning, secret scanning, and Dependabot across an organization's repositories, giving security teams a single place to assess posture.
explanationIncorrect: The Insights tab shows traffic and contribution analytics, not aggregated security alerts. The Actions tab lists workflow runs, not security findings. The Packages page manages published artifacts and has no security alert aggregation.

stem: Which feature lets maintainers privately collaborate on and disclose a vulnerability in their own project?

options.text: Repository security advisories with a temporary private fork
A public issue labeled security
A pinned Discussion
A protected branch

explanationCorrect: Repository security advisories provide a private space, including a temporary private fork, where maintainers can discuss, fix, and coordinate disclosure of a vulnerability before publishing.
explanationIncorrect: A public issue labeled security is visible to everyone, defeating the confidentiality needed before disclosure. A pinned Discussion is also public and not designed for coordinated vulnerability handling. A protected branch controls merges but offers no private collaboration or disclosure workflow.

stem: What is the purpose of a CodeQL analysis running on a schedule in addition to on pull requests?

options.text: To catch newly disclosed query improvements and drift on the default branch even without new PRs
To replace pull request analysis entirely
To reduce Actions minutes
To rotate secrets nightly

explanationCorrect: A scheduled scan re-analyzes the default branch periodically so that improved queries and issues not tied to a recent pull request are still surfaced, keeping the baseline current.
explanationIncorrect: It complements rather than replaces pull request analysis, which is needed to catch issues before merge. It does not reduce Actions minutes; running additional scheduled scans consumes more, not fewer. It has nothing to do with rotating secrets, which is a secret scanning concern, not a CodeQL schedule.

stem: Which feature allows security findings from external SAST tools to be centralized in the GitHub security tab?

options.text: Uploading SARIF results to code scanning
Attaching a PDF report to a release
Posting findings in Discussions
Committing a results.txt file

explanationCorrect: Code scanning accepts SARIF uploads, so results from third-party static analysis tools appear as alerts in the security tab alongside CodeQL findings.
explanationIncorrect: A PDF attached to a release is not parsed into code scanning alerts and cannot be triaged like them. Posting findings in Discussions leaves them as free-form text, not structured alerts. Committing a results.txt file does not register the findings with code scanning; the supported mechanism is SARIF upload.

stem: What does enabling GHAS on a private repository unlock that is not available without it?

options.text: Code scanning and secret scanning for that private repository
Free unlimited Actions minutes
Automatic code formatting
Unlimited storage for packages

explanationCorrect: For private repositories, code scanning and secret scanning are GHAS features, so enabling GHAS is what makes those security capabilities available there.
explanationIncorrect: GHAS does not grant free unlimited Actions minutes; compute billing is separate. It does not perform automatic code formatting, which is not a security feature. It does not provide unlimited package storage; packages are governed by their own storage and billing rules.

stem: Security overview offers enablement trends and alert metrics. How does this help a security program?

options.text: It shows which repositories have features enabled and how alerts are trending, guiding coverage and prioritization
It automatically fixes all open alerts
It replaces the need for branch protection
It compiles the application for release

explanationCorrect: By revealing enablement gaps and alert trends across repositories, Security overview helps teams decide where to turn on features and which risks to tackle first, driving measurable improvement.
explanationIncorrect: It does not automatically fix alerts; remediation still requires code or configuration changes. It does not replace branch protection, which enforces merge gates that a reporting view cannot. It does not compile the application; building for release is unrelated to a security reporting dashboard.

stem: Which statement about secret scanning coverage under GHAS is correct for private repositories?

options.text: Secret scanning for private repositories requires GHAS to be enabled
Secret scanning never works on private repositories
Secret scanning on private repositories is free without GHAS
Secret scanning requires disabling the dependency graph

explanationCorrect: On private repositories, secret scanning is part of GHAS, so it must be enabled through a GHAS license to protect those repositories.
explanationIncorrect: It does work on private repositories when GHAS is enabled, so the claim that it never works is false. It is not free without GHAS on private repositories; that free tier applies to public repositories. It has no dependence on disabling the dependency graph; the two features operate independently.
